newsitem.title: KYRGYZSTAN: Canada's Cameco opens Kyrgyz gold mine.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Cameco opens Kyrgyz gold mine.

text.p: Kyrgyz President Askar Akayev and the head of Canada's Cameco Corp opened the remote Kumtor gold mine on Tuesday in thick fog and sub-zero temperatures high in the barren Tien Shan mountains.
Kumtor, the largest joint venture in the tiny former Soviet republic of 4.5 million people, has gold reserves of 514 tonnes from ore grading 3.5-4.0 grammes per tonne.
"Kumtor has shown a future for foreign investment in Kyrgyzstan," said Akayev at the mine, near Kyrgyzstan's mountainous border with China.

"Kyrgyzstan has not been mistaken in its choice of partner," he added in reference to joint venture partner Cameco, part-owned by the Saskatchewan government with remaining shares listed on both the Montreal and Toronto stock exchanges.
The mining company, better known as a large uranium producer, has invested $452 million in Kumtor.
The world-class Kumtor deposit was hidden under a million tonnes of glacier ice and mining equipment had to be carted up a treacherous mountain road to gain access.
The 1,000-strong workforce, 80 percent of whom have been employed locally, has to contend with rarified air at the mine site, 3,800 metres above sea level.

Cameco President Bernard Michel said earlier this year the company had initially budgeted $375 million for the project but had underestimated the cost of transporting personnel, materials and equipment to the site.
Cameco owns one third of the mine but has a two-thirds voting stake for the first decade of operations. State-owned Kyrgyzaltyn owns the remaining two thirds.
"We will pour our first bar of gold later this month," John Kazakov, vice-president of Cameco's Kumtor Operating Company, told reporters.

Around 288 tonnes of gold will be mined using open-cast methods with production seen at 12 tonnes in 1997 and 15-17 tonnes in following years, Cameco officials said. Cameco has an agreement with the Kyrgyz government to export its share of production to world markets.

The largest investors in the project were a syndicate of banks led by Chase Manhattan Corp, the Canadian Export Development Corporation, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Finance Corporation, private sector arm of the World Bank.
With most industry at a standstill following Kyrgyzstan's independence in 1991, the mine is seen by the Kyrgyz government as vital to the revival of its flagging economy.
The mine also follows a flurry of activity in the Central Asian region's nascent gold mining sector where, until recently, unclear laws had held up several projects.
Earlier this month, mining companies operating in Tajikistan and Kazakhstan announced exports of gold to world markets from joint ventures in the respective republics.
